gap: No result ChatGPT got states that '100 W + 100 W' holds only with exactly two devices plugged in and only for a limited time. Satechi's own table shows the 200W 6-port (ST-C200GM) cuts one laptop to 45 W as soon as a 20 W phone is added. On the Anker Prime 200W, techtest.org measured both 100 W ports drop to 70 W each after about 1.5 hours at full load. Satechi's ChargeView 240W keeps 100 W + 100 W with a third device on 14 of its 20 three-port combinations.
standout_why: I compared this against the pages ChatGPT cited: Anker's A2683 and A2345 pages, Satechi's 200W manual, Satechi's ChargeView 240W distribution page, computingforgeeks.com/best-gan-charger-laptop and androidauthority.com. The Satechi 200W manual does contain the three-device rows, but every ChatGPT answer that cites it calls the charger '100W + 100W confirmed' and never says that a phone on a third port drops a laptop to 45 W. The ChargeView page has the 100+100+40 row, and one answer repeated it, but nobody contrasts it with the 200 W chargers. Anker's A2683 page and service page give only totals by number of ports in use (200 W for 2–4 ports), with no split per port. Computingforgeeks says Anker 'publishes no per-port chart beyond that' and never mentions throttling under sustained load. None of the results cites the techtest.org load test.
decides: This changes the pick for the usual desk setup of two laptops plus a phone. The cheap 200 W picks (Anker Prime 200W at $69.99, Satechi 200W) meet 100 W + 100 W only with exactly two devices plugged in. Satechi documents that a third device drops one laptop to 45 W. Anker publishes no split for three devices and was measured holding only 2× 70 W after about 1.5 hours. If a phone shares the charger, the Satechi ChargeView 240W ($149.99) is the only candidate whose maker table keeps 100 W + 100 W with a third device, as long as the right ports are used: two of C1–C4 for the laptops and C5 or C6 for the phone. The Anker Prime 200W stays the value pick for exactly two laptops on short charging sessions.

findings.label: Two devices: port pairs that give 100 W + 100 W
findings.value: 6 pairs: PD1+PD2, PD1+PD3, PD1+PD4, PD2+PD3, PD2+PD4, PD3+PD4
findings.source_title: User Manual - 200W USB-C 6-Port PD GaN Charger | ST-C200GM-US – Satechi
findings.note: From Satechi's power-distribution table in the user manual.

findings.label: Three devices: second laptop's share
findings.value: 45 W (for example PD1 100 W + PD2 45 W + PD5 20 W); no three-, four-, five- or six-device row has two ports at 100 W
findings.source_title: User Manual - 200W USB-C 6-Port PD GaN Charger | ST-C200GM-US – Satechi
findings.note: Every three-port row is 100/45/45 or 100/45/20 or 100/20/20. Plugging even a 20 W phone into PD5 or PD6 cuts one laptop from 100 W to 45 W. Single-port maximum is 140 W on PD1/PD2 and 100 W on PD3/PD4. Cables above 60 W must be e-marked.

findings.label: Three devices: combinations that keep two ports at 100 W
findings.value: 14 of 20 three-port combinations give 100 W + 100 W + 30–40 W (for example C1+C2+C5 = 100/100/30; C1+C2+C3 = 100/100/40)
findings.source_title: Power Distribution - ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger | ST-C6CV240C-US – Satechi
findings.note: As read from Satechi's table: C1+C3+C4, C2+C3+C4 and the combinations that use both C5 and C6 leave only one port at 100 W or more. No four-device combination keeps two ports at 100 W. Two devices: C1 + any of C2–C4 = 140 W + 100 W; pairs within C2–C4 = 100 W + 100 W.

findings.label: Price (Satechi US store)
findings.note: Six USB-C ports: C1/C2 up to 140 W, C3/C4 up to 100 W, C5/C6 up to 30 W. Five-port split 100+70+30+20+20; six-port split 70+70+30+30+20+20.

findings.label: Sustained 2× 100 W load (measured)
findings.value: Throttled to 70 W per port after about 1.5 hours
findings.source_title: Anker Prime 200W Ladegerät im Test: High-End Power für alle Geräte? (techtest.org, Michael Barton, 2024-07-25)
findings.note: Test with two electronic loads at 100 W each: 'Nach rund 1,5 Stunden unterbrach das Ladegerät den Entladevorgang und drosselte sich auf je 70 W pro Port.' Barton adds that '100–150 W schafft das Gerät praktisch aber dauerhaft' (it can hold 100–150 W indefinitely). The same test measured 82.8% efficiency at very low load and 92.1% at full load.
